power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Narrow-band display primaries increase observer metamerism, but to what extent does chromatic adaptation mitigate the perceptual consequences of these effects?
We simulated 10,000 individualized observers viewing real-world reflectances under varied illuminants and optimized a virtual RGB display to reproduce each observer's cone excitations.
Between-observer disagreement was quantified using ΔE′ in CAM16-UCS.
Without adaptation, metamerism increased as primaries narrowed, reaching a median ΔE′ of 4.8.
Increasing adaptation reduced metamerism monotonically: complete adaptation reduced observers' ΔE′ by a median of 40-67%, with the largest proportional reduction for the narrowest primaries.
Adaptation to shared stimuli may therefore align visual experiences across individuals.
Human colour vision begins with photon capture by three classes of cone photoreceptors: long-(L), middle-(M), and short-wavelength (S) sensitive cones.

Even among colour-normal observers, the spectral sensitivities that determine these cone excitations vary substantially across individuals, with important theoretical and practical consequences for colorimetry and image reproduction [1] [2] [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: Even among colour-normal observers, the spectral sensitivities that determine these cone excitations vary substantially across individuals, with important theoretical and practical consequences for colorimetry and image reproduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Cone fundamentals are defined at the cornea and thus include prereceptoral filtering, notably the crystalline lens and macular pigment.

Lens density varies markedly across observers and changes systematically with age, whereas macular pigment varies across observers and depends strongly on retinal location and thus on field size [6] [7].
text.formatted: Lens density varies markedly across observers and changes systematically with age, whereas macular pigment varies across observers and depends strongly on retinal location and thus on field size <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Variability also originates in the cones themselves: photopigment optical density differs between observers [8], and L/M cone peak wavelength and bandwidth vary with opsin polymorphisms, gene recombination, and hybrid pigments [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14].

text.text: Psychophysical estimates in observers of known genotype confirm systematic differences in cone spectral sensitivities among colour-normal observers [15] and with retinal eccentricity [6].
text.formatted: Psychophysical estimates in observers of known genotype confirm systematic differences in cone spectral sensitivities among colour-normal observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> and with retinal eccentricity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: To represent these physiological sources of variability in a usable form, parameterized observer models generate individualized cone fundamentals from a common physiological basis [6], and the Individual Colorimetric Observer Model of Asano et al. enables large-scale simulations of individualized colorimetry [16].

text.text: Complementary formulae, such as those of Stockman and Rider, facilitate efficient generation of standard and individual corneal cone sensitivities [17].
text.formatted: Complementary formulae, such as those of Stockman and Rider, facilitate efficient generation of standard and individual corneal cone sensitivities <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Recent CIE discussions further emphasize the long-term goal of basing colorimetry on cone fundamentals and the importance of incorporating individual variations [18].
text.formatted: Recent CIE discussions further emphasize the long-term goal of basing colorimetry on cone fundamentals and the importance of incorporating individual variations <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Inter-individual differences in cone fundamentals imply observer-dependent colour experience in display and lighting devices.
A long-standing manifestation is observer metamerism: spectra that match for one observer may fail to match for another when reproduced by a fixed set of primaries.
Observer metamerism has long been formalized in colorimetry through metamerism indices and their practical interpretation [19] [20].
text.formatted: Observer metamerism has long been formalized in colorimetry through metamerism indices and their practical interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: In the display domain, it has been quantified for commercial devices and a wide range of viewing conditions, including different primary sets and white points, technology comparisons (e.g., LCD vs OLED), daylight-mimicking but spectrally non-smooth LED illumination, and widegamut/HDR regimes [21] [22] [23] [24] [25].
text.formatted: In the display domain, it has been quantified for commercial devices and a wide range of viewing conditions, including different primary sets and white points, technology comparisons (e.g., LCD vs OLED), daylight-mimicking but spectrally non-smooth LED illumination, and widegamut/HDR regimes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Sensitivity-style indices and measurement standards have also been proposed to support display design and evaluation [26] [27] [28] [29] [30].
text.formatted: Sensitivity-style indices and measurement standards have also been proposed to support display design and evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Across many studies, a consistent finding is that spectrally narrow primaries tend to exacerbate observer metamerism.

Intuitively, narrowing a primary concentrates power into a smaller wavelength region, so the resulting cone excitations become more sensitive to observer-specific differences in spectral sensitivity at those wavelengths.
Recent work has also shown that primary peak wavelengths and primary-set design influence both colour matching accuracy and the magnitude of observer variability [31] [32] [33].
text.formatted: Recent work has also shown that primary peak wavelengths and primary-set design influence both colour matching accuracy and the magnitude of observer variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: However, despite substantial inter-individual differences at the receptor level, colour appearance is often reported to be relatively stable across observers in everyday viewing, suggesting that downstream compensation and adaptation buffer spectral sensitivity differences [2, 34].
text.formatted: However, despite substantial inter-individual differences at the receptor level, colour appearance is often reported to be relatively stable across observers in everyday viewing, suggesting that downstream compensation and adaptation buffer spectral sensitivity differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref>.

text.text: This stability is striking in anomalous trichromacy: although anomalous trichromats have markedly altered L/M sensitivities, their subjective colour experience and neural responses can show substantial compensation [35] [36] [37].
text.formatted: This stability is striking in anomalous trichromacy: although anomalous trichromats have markedly altered L/M sensitivities, their subjective colour experience and neural responses can show substantial compensation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: For displays, simulations and measurements suggest that prolonged viewing can partially normalize visual experiences through chromatic adaptation and related gain-control mechanisms [38] [39] [40] [41].
text.formatted: For displays, simulations and measurements suggest that prolonged viewing can partially normalize visual experiences through chromatic adaptation and related gain-control mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: This study poses two questions: how large is observer metamerism before any chromatic adaptation; and how much of it is removed by chromatic adaptation whose degree rises from none (D = 0) to complete (D = 1).

We generated 10,000 individual observers using Asano's model and a family of RGB displays whose primary bandwidth varied from broadband to narrowband, and rendered test surfaces under three illuminant classes -CIE daylight [42], smooth artificial, and spectrally peaky artificial.
text.formatted: We generated 10,000 individual observers using Asano's model and a family of RGB displays whose primary bandwidth varied from broadband to narrowband, and rendered test surfaces under three illuminant classes -CIE daylight <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>, smooth artificial, and spectrally peaky artificial.

text.text: Observer metamerism is quantified in CAM16-UCS -the perceptually uniform space of the CIE's current colour-appearance model and its recommended representation for evaluating perceptual colour differences [43] [44] -as the distance between the colour reproduced for an individual observer and the colour reproduced for the reference (CIE 1931) observer.
text.formatted: Observer metamerism is quantified in CAM16-UCS -the perceptually uniform space of the CIE's current colour-appearance model and its recommended representation for evaluating perceptual colour differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref> -as the distance between the colour reproduced for an individual observer and the colour reproduced for the reference (CIE 1931) observer.

text.text: We measure the pre-adaptation metamerism, specifying how large it is and which surfaces it affects most.
We then show how chromatic adaptation reduces the perceptual difference as the degree of adaptation rises from none to complete.

text.text: It is worth being explicit about what this construction means.
By design every observer is looking at a perfect match: in that observer's own cone space the display reproduces the world spectrum exactly, so no individual perceives an error.
The disagreement lives strictly between observers, and it becomes visible only once their matches are read out in a common space.
Observer metamerism in this framework is therefore a read-out phenomenon -not that any observer's percept is wrong, but that the physical stimuli different observers accept as correct are different.
To quantify the magnitude of these differences, we could use a radiometric quantity (e.g. the rms difference in SPD).
However, since we are interested in the perceptual significance of these differences, we quantify observer metamerism in CAM16-UCS, the perceptually uniform form of CIECAM16 [43].

For a fixed set of display primaries, Γi→std depends only on the cone fundamentals of the two observers.
It describes how the three cone excitations of observer i are linearly combined to predict the corresponding excitations of the standard observer.
The diagonal elements ΓLL, ΓMM, and ΓSS represent within-cone-class gains: for example, ΓLL describes the contribution of observer i's L-cone excitation to the standard observer's L-cone excitation.
The six off-diagonal elements -ΓLM, ΓLS, ΓML, ΓMS, ΓSL, and ΓSM -represent mixing between different cone classes.
This decomposition provides an approximate diagnostic of whether a von Kries correction can account for differences between observers.
Because a von Kries transform applies an independent gain to each cone-like channel, it can account for the diagonal terms but not the off-diagonal cross-cone terms.
Successful correction therefore requires both small off-diagonal terms and an appropriate choice of white point, such that the resulting channel gains match the diagonal terms reasonably well.

text.text: A gain is diagonal, so it can only correct differences between observers that are themselves diagonal -a rescaling of each cone channel -and not any mixing between channels.

To test how far real observer differences meet that condition, we formed for every observer the 3 × 3 matrix Γ that maps that observer's LMS cone excitations onto the reference observer's for a display with the same primaries (Eq. 8), and plotted the distribution of each of its nine entries across the 10,000 observers.
A diagonal entry (ΓLL, ΓMM, ΓSS) is the gain on one cone channel; an off-diagonal entry is cross-talk -one observer's cone signal leaking into a different channel of the reference observer.

If observer differences were a pure per-channel gain -the form a von Kries / CAT16 white adaptation can undo -every offdiagonal entry would be zero and only the three diagonal entries would move; for the reference observer Γ is exactly the identity (dashed lines).

The Γ matrices calculated across the population of 10,000 simulated observers are indeed dominated by the diagonal at every bandwidth: the diagonal entries cluster near unity (mean ΓLL = 1.12, ΓMM = 0.95, ΓSS = 0.99 at σ = 5 nm) while every off-diagonal entry is small (mean ΓLM = -0.136, ΓLS = -0.015; ΓML = 0.050, ΓMS = -0.038; and ΓSL = -0.0005, ΓSM = 0.002).
A per-channel gain is therefore a well-matched model of the difference between observers -the structural reason a white-anchored diagonal removes most of the metamerism.
Primary bandwidth shifts this balance.

Broadening the primaries from σ = 5 to 20 nm enlarges every off-diagonal entry -the cross-talk no gain can absorb (ΓLM -0.136 → -0.150, ΓML 0.050 → 0.066, ΓMS -0.038 → -0.048, ΓSM 0.002 → 0.005) -so narrow primaries leave the map more diagonal, and better matched to gain control.

The between-observer spread of the diagonal entries, meanwhile, does not uniformly shrink when the primaries narrow: from σ = 20 to 5 nm the standard deviation across observers is unchanged for ΓLL (0.10 at both bandwidths), falls for ΓMM (0.061 to 0.041) but rises for ΓSS (0.021 to 0.034), because with near-monochromatic primaries ΓSS is approximately the ratio of standard to individual S-cone sensitivity at 450 nm, a wavelength where macular and lens pigmentation differ most across observers.

Narrow primaries therefore concentrate the between-observer differences into the diagonal gains while suppressing the off-diagonal cross-talk, which is why von Kries-type adaptation is proportionally most effective at the narrowest primaries.
Our simulations recapitulate a clear trade-off in display spectral design: narrowing the primary bandwidth expands the attainable gamut but increases observer metamerism before adaptation.
Much of this increase, however, was reduced by white-anchored chromatic adaptation, particularly for the narrowest primaries.
At σ = 5 nm, adaptation reduced metamerism by approximately 67% under peaky illumination and 60% under daylight, compared with 58% and 55%, respectively, at σ = 20 nm.

The cross-observer transformations were also more nearly diagonal for narrower primaries, especially for entries where S-cones are involved (Fig. 6), indicating that the resulting observer differences were better approximated by channel-wise gain control.

text.text: Our results suggest that adaptation state is an important additional dimension: two displays with similar pre-adaptation metamerism could differ substantially in post-adaptation behaviour if their adopted whites differ in stability.

Recent display-side corrections and observer-specific colour-management workflows [62] [63] [64] [65] [66] [67] would likewise interact with the assumed adaptation state -whether observers are fully adapted to the display white, only partially adapted, or repeatedly re-adapting under mixed viewing.

text.text: A natural concern is how far our results depend on the specific adapting white.
We anchored adaptation to each observer's own reproduction of the highest-luminance (display-white) surface, but other plausible scene statistics could serve as the anchor.

We therefore repeated the full-adaptation analysis with the adapting white defined instead as the mean cone excitation over the surface set (a grey-world white, which in effect weights every surface by its luminance) or as the mean chromaticity of the surfaces.

Figure 7 shows that both alternatives change the median reduction at D = 1 by at most five percentage points in any illuminant class or bandwidth, in most cases slightly upward, and that the benefit still decreases with bandwidth in every class.

text.text: This optimized white (dotted lines in Fig. 7) raises the median reduction at D = 1, pooled over illuminant classes, to 72%, 71% and 65% at σ = 5, 10 and 20 nm, so the highest-luminance anchor already captures roughly 80% of the achievable reduction.

text.text: The bound is not itself attainable in real viewing -an observer cannot choose an adaptation state, which is set by the scene -but together with the alternative anchors it shows that the conclusions do not hinge on how the white is estimated.
Several limitations are worth noting.
Chromatic adaptation was modelled within the CIECAM16 framework, using its CAT16 white-anchored gain control rather than an ad hoc correction.
This reduces concerns associated with adopting an overly simplified adaptation stage, as the model provides a standardized and perceptually motivated account of chromatic adaptation.

Nevertheless, it remains an approximation based on a single adopted white and a single degree-of-adaptation parameter, whereas biological chromatic adaptation is likely to involve additional spatial, contextual, and temporal mechanisms operating over multiple timescales [41, [69] [70].

text.text: As with much of the observer-metamerism literature, the present evidence is based on simulation.
Psychophysical validation is therefore desirable, particularly because task demands and decision criteria may modulate the perceptual consequences of physical mismatches.

Recent experimental paradigms and task-calibrated failure indices could be used to test these predictions and quantify the interaction between primary bandwidth and adaptation directly [71] [72] [73] [74].

text.text: Finally, the examination of these effects may be extended to multi-primary and HDR conditions, where spectral design and luminance may both influence metamerism and tolerance thresholds [25, [75] [76], and where perceptual metrics beyond CAM16-UCS, including modern visualdifference predictors, may correspond more closely to the visibility of differences [77] [78].

text.text: Using 10,000 individualized observers and a stimulus set based on reproducing real-world spectra of surfaces viewed under three CCT-matched illuminant classes, we find that pre-adaptation observer metamerism on a narrow-primary display, scored in CAM16-UCS, is governed by the spectral difference between the world spectrum and its display reproduction -largest under smooth daylight and at the narrowest primaries.

As every observer's degree of adaptation rises from none to complete, this metamerism falls monotonically; complete adaptation to each observer's own white removes 54-67% of it at σ = 5 nm, somewhat more than at the broadest primaries, so under adapted viewing narrowband primaries are less detrimental than their unadapted reputation suggests.

The adopted white point and the degree of adaptation -the adaptation state -therefore govern observer metamerism under adapted viewing, and are the appropriate focus when interpreting observer-metamerism indices and evaluating narrow-band primary designs.
